section_1.title: The Hook: The Map Dilemma
section_1.content: Introduce the concept that the 'coordinates' of a point depend entirely on the 'map' (basis) you are using. Use a narrative approach to show that the same physical location can have different numerical labels.
section_1.example: Two explorers, Alice and Bob, are in a desert. Alice uses a standard North-East grid. Bob uses a grid aligned with a slanted canyon and a distant oasis. They are looking at the same treasure chest. Alice says it's at (3, 4), but Bob needs to know what that means in his 'slanted' coordinate system.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Refresher: What is a Basis?
section_2.content: Quickly review that a basis is a set of linearly independent vectors that span a space. Visually represent the Standard Basis (i, j) as a rigid square grid.
section_2.example: Show a 2D plane with unit vectors e1 (1,0) and e2 (0,1). Demonstrate how any vector 'v' is just a recipe: 3 steps of e1 and 2 steps of e2.

section_3.title: The New Perspective: Non-Standard Basis
section_3.content: Introduce a new basis 'B' consisting of two vectors, b1 and b2, that are not at right angles. Graphically overlay a 'skewed' or 'tilted' grid on top of the standard grid to show how space is re-measured.
section_3.example: Visual: A robot is programmed to move along a basis B where b1 = (2, 1) and b2 = (-1, 1). Show the robot's world-view as a diamond-shaped grid instead of a square one.

section_4.title: The Bridge: The Change of Basis Matrix
section_4.content: Explain the 'Transition Matrix' (P). This matrix acts as a translator. Key concept: The columns of the transition matrix from B to the standard basis are simply the coordinates of b1 and b2 written in the standard basis.
section_4.example: To translate Bob's coordinates back to Alice's, we build a matrix P where Column 1 is Bob's first vector (2, 1) and Column 2 is Bob's second vector (-1, 1). Animation shows the standard grid morphing/stretching into Bob's grid.

section_5.title: The Mathematical Transformation
section_5.content: Present the core formula: [v]standard = P * [v]B and [v]B = P⁻¹ * [v]standard. Emphasize that P inverse is the 'decoder' that takes us from the standard world into the custom basis world.
section_5.example: Calculation: If a point is at (1, 1) in Bob's slanted system, what is it for Alice? We multiply the matrix P by the vector [1, 1] to get the result (1, 2) in Alice's standard system.

section_6.title: Real-World Application: Computer Graphics
section_6.content: Show how change of basis is used in gaming or CGI to calculate how a character 'sees' an object compared to how the 'world' sees it (Camera Space vs. World Space).
section_6.example: A flying dragon (the character) has its own forward/up/side basis. As it tilts its wings, its internal basis changes. To render the sun in the dragon's eyes, the computer performs a Change of Basis from 'World Coordinates' to 'Dragon Coordinates'.

section_7.title: Summary & Key Takeaway
section_7.content: Wrap up by reinforcing that a vector is an absolute 'arrow' in space; only its 'name' (coordinates) changes when we change our perspective (basis).
section_7.example: Animation: The treasure chest stays in the same spot while the grid lines under it spin and stretch, showing the coordinates changing from (3,4) to (1.5, 2.2) while the physical location remains fixed.

section_1.title: The Hook: The Map Dilemma
section_1.content: Introduce the concept that the 'coordinates' of a point depend entirely on the 'map' (basis) you are using. Use a narrative approach to show that the same physical location can have different numerical labels.
section_1.example: Two explorers, Alice and Bob, are in a desert. Alice uses a standard North-East grid. Bob uses a grid aligned with a slanted canyon and a distant oasis. They are looking at the same treasure chest. Alice says it's at (3, 4), but Bob needs to know what that means in his 'slanted' coordinate system.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Refresher: What is a Basis?
section_2.content: Quickly review that a basis is a set of linearly independent vectors that span a space. Visually represent the Standard Basis (i, j) as a rigid square grid.
section_2.example: Show a 2D plane with unit vectors e1 (1,0) and e2 (0,1). Demonstrate how any vector 'v' is just a recipe: 3 steps of e1 and 2 steps of e2.

section_3.title: The New Perspective: Non-Standard Basis
section_3.content: Introduce a new basis 'B' consisting of two vectors, b1 and b2, that are not at right angles. Graphically overlay a 'skewed' or 'tilted' grid on top of the standard grid to show how space is re-measured.
section_3.example: Visual: A robot is programmed to move along a basis B where b1 = (2, 1) and b2 = (-1, 1). Show the robot's world-view as a diamond-shaped grid instead of a square one.

section_4.title: The Bridge: The Change of Basis Matrix
section_4.content: Explain the 'Transition Matrix' (P). This matrix acts as a translator. Key concept: The columns of the transition matrix from B to the standard basis are simply the coordinates of b1 and b2 written in the standard basis.
section_4.example: To translate Bob's coordinates back to Alice's, we build a matrix P where Column 1 is Bob's first vector (2, 1) and Column 2 is Bob's second vector (-1, 1). Animation shows the standard grid morphing/stretching into Bob's grid.

section_5.title: The Mathematical Transformation
section_5.content: Present the core formula: [v]standard = P * [v]B and [v]B = P⁻¹ * [v]standard. Emphasize that P inverse is the 'decoder' that takes us from the standard world into the custom basis world.
section_5.example: Calculation: If a point is at (1, 1) in Bob's slanted system, what is it for Alice? We multiply the matrix P by the vector [1, 1] to get the result (1, 2) in Alice's standard system.

section_6.title: Real-World Application: Computer Graphics
section_6.content: Show how change of basis is used in gaming or CGI to calculate how a character 'sees' an object compared to how the 'world' sees it (Camera Space vs. World Space).
section_6.example: A flying dragon (the character) has its own forward/up/side basis. As it tilts its wings, its internal basis changes. To render the sun in the dragon's eyes, the computer performs a Change of Basis from 'World Coordinates' to 'Dragon Coordinates'.

section_7.title: Summary & Key Takeaway
section_7.content: Wrap up by reinforcing that a vector is an absolute 'arrow' in space; only its 'name' (coordinates) changes when we change our perspective (basis).
section_7.example: Animation: The treasure chest stays in the same spot while the grid lines under it spin and stretch, showing the coordinates changing from (3,4) to (1.5, 2.2) while the physical location remains fixed.

section_1.title: The Hook: The Map Dilemma
lecture_lines: Imagine one treasure chest, but two different maps.
Alice uses a standard North-East grid.
Bob's map is tilted along a canyon.
animations: Show Alice's white (#FFFFFF) standard grid over a desert background; place a treasure chest at (3, 4).
Overlay Bob's slanted yellow (#FFFF00) grid, keeping the treasure chest at the same physical location.
Highlight the coordinate (3, 4) in Alice's grid and a different coordinate pair in Bob's grid.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Refresher: What is a Basis?
lecture_lines: A basis is a set of building-block vectors.
Standard basis vectors are unit-length and perpendicular.
Every point is a unique recipe of vectors.
animations: Display the standard basis: unit vectors e1 (1,0) in red (#FF0000) and e2 (0,1) in blue (#0000FF) on a white grid (#FFFFFF).
Create vector 'v' from (0,0) to (3,2) in cyan (#00FFFF).
Trace the path to 'v' using 3 red (#FF0000) e1 steps and 2 blue (#0000FF) e2 steps.

section_3.title: The New Perspective: Non-Standard Basis
lecture_lines: Bases don't have to be square.
We can define space using any independent vectors.
This creates a custom, skewed coordinate grid.
animations: Introduce basis vectors b1 (2,1) in light green (#90EE90) and b2 (-1,1) in orange (#FFA500) on the standard grid.
Fade out the standard grid and fade in a skewed light green (#90EE90) grid aligned with b1 and b2.
Show a small robot icon moving along the skewed grid to coordinates (1,1).

section_4.title: The Bridge: The Change of Basis Matrix
lecture_lines: A Change of Basis matrix translates between systems.
It maps Bob's coordinates back to Alice's.
The columns are Bob's vectors in Alice's language.
This matrix morphs standard grids into Bob's.
We call this transformation matrix P.
animations: Show the Change of Basis Matrix P = [[2, -1], [1, 1]] with columns colored light green (#90EE90) and orange (#FFA500).
Animate the standard white grid (#FFFFFF) morphing into the skewed light green (#90EE90) grid.
Highlight how the columns of P correspond exactly to the coordinates of b1 and b2 in the standard grid.

section_5.title: The Mathematical Transformation
lecture_lines: Multiply P by Bob's vector to find Alice's.
Use the inverse of P for the reverse.
P-inverse decodes standard vectors into custom bases.
It transforms the perspective, not the vector itself.
Math allows us to swap viewpoints instantly.
animations: Display the core formula [v]std = P * [v]B in white (#FFFFFF) at the top of the screen.
Substitute [1,1] for [v]B and multiply by matrix P to calculate the result (1,2).
Simultaneously show the vector at (1,1) in the skewed grid and its transformation to (1,2) in the standard grid.

section_6.title: Real-World Application: Computer Graphics
lecture_lines: Graphics engines use this to render 3D scenes.
Characters have their own local basis.
The world has a global standard basis.
Moving cameras requires a change of basis.
This aligns the world with your view.
animations: Illustrate a 'Dragon' icon with its own local axes (forward/up) in a 'World' grid.
Rotate the Dragon and its local axes to show how its perspective changes relative to the World grid.
Project a 'Sun' object's position onto the Dragon's local axes, showing its local coordinates change during the rotation.

section_7.title: Summary & Key Takeaway
lecture_lines: Vectors are absolute arrows in physical space.
Coordinates are just labels relative to a basis.
Change your basis to see the world differently.
animations: Show a static cyan (#00FFFF) arrow (vector) pointing to a fixed point in space.
Continuously rotate and scale the underlying grid lines beneath the fixed arrow.
Display changing coordinate labels (x,y) that update as the grid moves, while the arrow remains stationary.

outline.title: Prerequisite Refresher: What is a Basis?
outline.content: Quickly review that a basis is a set of linearly independent vectors that span a space. Visually represent the Standard Basis (i, j) as a rigid square grid.
outline.example: Show a 2D plane with unit vectors e1 (1,0) and e2 (0,1). Demonstrate how any vector 'v' is just a recipe: 3 steps of e1 and 2 steps of e2.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Refresher: What is a Basis?
lecture_lines: A basis is a set of building-block vectors.
Standard basis vectors are unit-length and perpendicular.
Every point is a unique recipe of vectors.
animations: Display the standard basis: unit vectors e1 (1,0) in red (#FF0000) and e2 (0,1) in blue (#0000FF) on a white grid (#FFFFFF).
Create vector 'v' from (0,0) to (3,2) in cyan (#00FFFF).
Trace the path to 'v' using 3 red (#FF0000) e1 steps and 2 blue (#0000FF) e2 steps.

outline.title: Real-World Application: Computer Graphics
outline.content: Show how change of basis is used in gaming or CGI to calculate how a character 'sees' an object compared to how the 'world' sees it (Camera Space vs. World Space).
outline.example: A flying dragon (the character) has its own forward/up/side basis. As it tilts its wings, its internal basis changes. To render the sun in the dragon's eyes, the computer performs a Change of Basis from 'World Coordinates' to 'Dragon Coordinates'.

storyboard.title: Real-World Application: Computer Graphics
lecture_lines: Graphics engines use this to render 3D scenes.
Characters have their own local basis.
The world has a global standard basis.
Moving cameras requires a change of basis.
This aligns the world with your view.
animations: Illustrate a 'Dragon' icon with its own local axes (forward/up) in a 'World' grid.
Rotate the Dragon and its local axes to show how its perspective changes relative to the World grid.
Project a 'Sun' object's position onto the Dragon's local axes, showing its local coordinates change during the rotation.

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout(
            "Prerequisite Refresher: What is a Basis?", 
            [
                "- A basis is a set of building-block vectors.",
                "- Standard basis vectors are unit-length and perpendicular.",
                "- Every point is a unique recipe of vectors."
            ]
        )

        # Pre-define colors
        COLOR_E1 = "#FF0000"
        COLOR_E2 = "#0000FF"
        COLOR_V = "#00FFFF"
        COLOR_GRID = "#FFFFFF"

        # Create coordinate system on the right side
        # Placing plane in area A1 to F6
        plane = NumberPlane(
            x_range=[-1, 5, 1],
            y_range=[-1, 4, 1],
            background_line_style={
                "stroke_color": COLOR_GRID,
                "stroke_width": 1,
                "stroke_opacity": 0.3
            },
            axis_config={"stroke_color": COLOR_GRID}
        )
        self.place_in_area(plane, 'A1', 'F6', scale_factor=0.7)
        
        # Helper to get point in plane's local coordinate system
        def p2c(x, y):
            return plane.coords_to_point(x, y)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        e1 = Arrow(p2c(0, 0), p2c(1, 0), buff=0, color=COLOR_E1)
        e2 = Arrow(p2c(0, 0), p2c(0, 1), buff=0, color=COLOR_E2)
        
        e1_label = MathTex(r"\hat{e}_1", color=COLOR_E1, font_size=24)
        e2_label = MathTex(r"\hat{e}_2", color=COLOR_E2, font_size=24)
        
        # Position labels near vectors
        e1_label.next_to(e1, DOWN, buff=0.1)
        e2_label.next_to(e2, LEFT, buff=0.1)

        self.play(Create(plane))
        self.play(GrowArrow(e1), GrowArrow(e2), Write(e1_label), Write(e2_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        # Highlight unit length and perpendicularity
        right_angle = RightAngle(e1, e2, length=0.2, color=WHITE)
        
        self.play(Create(right_angle))
        self.play(Indicate(e1), Indicate(e2))
        self.wait(1)
        self.play(FadeOut(right_angle))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color(YELLOW)

        # Vector v = 3*e1 + 2*e2
        v_vec = Arrow(p2c(0, 0), p2c(3, 2), buff=0, color=COLOR_V)
        v_label = MathTex(r"\vec{v}", color=COLOR_V, font_size=24).next_to(v_vec.get_end(), UR, buff=0.1)

        # Trace path
        path_e1_1 = Arrow(p2c(0, 0), p2c(1, 0), buff=0, color=COLOR_E1, stroke_width=2)
        path_e1_2 = Arrow(p2c(1, 0), p2c(2, 0), buff=0, color=COLOR_E1, stroke_width=2)
        path_e1_3 = Arrow(p2c(2, 0), p2c(3, 0), buff=0, color=COLOR_E1, stroke_width=2)
        
        path_e2_1 = Arrow(p2c(3, 0), p2c(3, 1), buff=0, color=COLOR_E2, stroke_width=2)
        path_e2_2 = Arrow(p2c(3, 1), p2c(3, 2), buff=0, color=COLOR_E2, stroke_width=2)

        self.play(GrowArrow(v_vec), Write(v_label))
        self.wait(0.5)
        
        # Show the "recipe"
        self.play(Create(path_e1_1))
        self.play(Create(path_e1_2))
        self.play(Create(path_e1_3))
        self.play(Create(path_e2_1))
        self.play(Create(path_e2_2))
        
        self.wait(2)
        
        # Clean up or finalize
        self.lecture[2].set_color(WHITE)
        self.wait(1)
